content: The attack rate of tuberculosis (TB) has been extensively studied in various populations and settings. For example, a 1960 report in the Bulletin of the World Health Organization analyzed TB transmission dynamics. Updated and consolidated guidelines for the programmatic management of latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) have been developed, including evidence-to-decision frameworks and GRADE tables. In Edinburgh, a 1958 study analyzed 3,485 TB contacts from 1954–1955, providing insights into transmission patterns. Similarly, research in Uganda has examined whole blood interferon-gamma responses to Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens in young household contacts of TB patients, highlighting immune responses in high-risk groups. In Indonesia, a 2015 study assessed the risk of TB infection and disease among children identified through community-based contact screening. High TB prevalence has been documented among children exposed to drug-resistant TB at home, as shown in a 2014 study in Pakistan. In Kampala, Uganda, a longitudinal household contact study identified clinical and epidemiological characteristics of individuals resistant to M. tuberculosis infection. Another study in Tanzania evaluated Mantoux skin test reactivity among household contacts of HIV-infected and uninfected TB patients. The impact of HIV on TB transmission has been a focus of several studies. For instance, a 1994 study in Kenya demonstrated that HIV-1 increases the infectiousness of TB. Similarly, a 2000 study in the Dominican Republic found that HIV-infected TB patients are more likely to transmit the disease. Research has also highlighted discordant T-cell responses in individuals recently exposed to household TB, as seen in a 2009 study in South Africa. Household contact investigations in Uganda have provided valuable data on TB transmission dynamics. A 1961 ten-year survey in the UK examined pulmonary TB in contacts, while a 2016 study in Zambia assessed TB prevalence in the context of HIV. National TB prevalence surveys in countries like Cambodia, Myanmar, Tanzania, Ethiopia, and Laos have further contributed to understanding the burden of TB. The diagnosis and management of LTBI remain critical challenges. Studies have compared the performance of tuberculin skin tests (TST) and interferon-gamma release assays (IGRA) in high TB-burden settings. For example, a 2011 South African study evaluated these tests in predicting TB disease in adolescents. Research has also explored the cost-effectiveness of shorter LTBI treatment regimens, such as a 12-dose combination of rifapentine and isoniazid. Efforts to prevent TB in high-risk populations, including children, healthcare workers, and people living with HIV, have been informed by randomized clinical trials and systematic reviews. For instance, a 2014 trial demonstrated the efficacy of isoniazid plus antiretroviral therapy in preventing TB among HIV-infected individuals. Studies have also examined the effectiveness of different LTBI treatment regimens, such as a 9-month isoniazid course versus shorter regimens combining isoniazid and rifampin. The management of multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) poses additional challenges. Research has investigated the transmission of MDR-TB to close contacts and the effectiveness of prophylactic treatments, such as moxifloxacin, in preventing MDR-TB. In summary, a wealth of research has advanced our understanding of TB transmission, diagnosis, and management, particularly in high-risk populations and settings. These findings underscore the need for targeted interventions, robust screening strategies, and effective treatment regimens to control TB and prevent its spread.
